newsitem.title: USA: Redskins' owner Jack Kent Cooke dies.
newsitem.headline: Redskins' owner Jack Kent Cooke dies.

text.p: Jack Kent Cooke, owner of the Washington Redskins football team and the head of a multimillion dollar business empire, died Sunday, a hospital spokeswoman said. He was 84.

Cooke, who started his career as a door-to-door encyclopaedia salesman, was worth an estimated $825 million. The Redskins won three Super Bowl championships during his 23-year tenure and were due to move to a new 78,000-seat stadium this fall in suburban Maryland.
George Washington University Hospital spokeswoman Merle Goldberg said Cooke was pronounced dead at 12:09 p.m. EDT from congestive heart failure resulting from heart disease.
The Canadian-born Cooke bought a radio station when he was 25 and, after acquiring newspapers and magazines, was a millionaire at age 30.
A pioneer in cable televsion, Cooke became a U.S. citizen in 1960. He made $500 million in the 1980s from the sale of cable systems.
His holdings included the Chrysler Building in New York.
President Clinton mourned the death of Cooke, the White House said.

"Hillary and I were saddened to learn of the death of Jack Kent Cooke. His straight-shooting style and love of the fans earned him respect and admiration throughout the sports world. Our thoughts and prayers are with his family at this time," the president said in a statement.
Cooke became the majority owner of the Redskins in 1974 and invested $360 million of his own money in the stadium project.
In his 23 years as owner, the Redskins were 223-151 with three Super Bowl titles, four NFC Championships and 11 playoff appearances.
He was the owner of the Los Angeles Lakers' basketball team in the 1970s and 1980s and also operated the Toronto Maple Leafs, a minor league baseball team, in the 1950s.
In 1967, as chairman of the NBA's Lakers and NHL's Los Angeles Kings, Cooke built the Los Angeles Forum, the first privately funded indoor arena in the United States.
Cooke was the owner of the world champion 1971-72 Lakers team that recorded an NBA-record 33-game winning streak.
Cooke traded for superstar centre Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and drafted and signed superstar guard Magic Johnson to provide a foundation of Laker championship teams in the 1980s.
Cooke also owned the Los Angeles Daily News.
